abstracts.title: Microscope inspection of alloy coupons
abstracts.abstract: Hairline defects in polished alloy coupons can escape a manual microscope inspection when lighting changes between sessions. In materials science, we trained a convolutional neural network on the AlloyScope-120 dataset to classify cropped images as scratched, pitted, or clear. The test partition held out entire coupons so that nearby crops could not appear on both sides of the split. We inspected disagreements under a second lamp setting and found that edges near the specimen holder were especially troublesome. The experiment uses fictional images and illustrates why specimen-level splits matter.

abstracts.title: Velocity snapshots in a stepped channel
abstracts.abstract: A separated shear layer downstream of a channel step produces velocity structures that recur at several scales. This fluid mechanics study uses proper orthogonal decomposition on the StepFlow-240 dataset of two-dimensional velocity snapshots. Each snapshot is centered using a training-set mean before computing modes. We compare reconstructions using four, eight, and twelve modes at the same set of downstream locations. A secondary visualization overlays the mean reattachment line to help readers interpret the modes. Snapshot order and sensor calibration are frozen before comparing reconstruction errors across the three truncation levels.

abstracts.title: Predicting seedling cover after rain
abstracts.abstract: In ecology, we used a random forest and the MesaPlots-64 dataset to predict seedling cover in dryland restoration plots after a short rain event. Inputs include shade fraction, surface gravel cover, and soil moisture recorded at the time of the survey. We grouped neighboring plots into blocks so that held-out plots were spatially separated from training plots. The prediction target is the fraction of ground covered by seedlings on the following visit. A simple median predictor serves as a reference, and feature rankings are interpreted cautiously because the measurements are correlated.

abstracts.title: Estimating bus arrival delays
abstracts.abstract: This transportation study applies gradient-boosted trees to the HarborBus-30 dataset, a fictional collection of scheduled and observed bus arrivals from thirty weekdays. We estimate lateness at the next stop using the departure delay, stop spacing, and a coarse time-of-day indicator. Complete service days are held out to avoid sharing closely related runs across training and testing. A schedule-only baseline helps separate predictable timetable errors from unusual congestion. We report errors by route segment and compare the morning peak with midday service so that a single average cannot hide poor behavior on a busy corridor.

abstracts.title: A closed-form heat transfer check
abstracts.abstract: In thermal engineering, we use the finite difference method to approximate the transient temperature in an insulated slab with a prescribed initial profile. The reference curve is evaluated directly from the stated analytical solution at each grid location. This is a numerical verification exercise and no dataset is specified. We halve the mesh spacing and reduce the time step according to the explicit stability limit. The reported quantity is the maximum error at a fixed physical time. We compare the decrease in error against the expected discretization order and keep all boundary conditions unchanged.

abstracts.title: Indexing phrases in municipal minutes
abstracts.abstract: For a digital humanities study we applied logistic regression to the CouncilPages-90 dataset to label short passages from fictional city council minutes as budget, zoning, or public comment. The features are word counts after a fixed stopword filter. Whole meetings are assigned to either training or test so that recurring speakers cannot split a single discussion across partitions. We inspect troublesome phrases that appear in more than one category, including references to zoning fees. A small hand-audited subset is used to check that the passage labels follow the stated topic definitions consistently.

abstracts.title: Separating cloud and surface signals
abstracts.abstract: In remote sensing, we trained a U-Net to identify cloud-covered pixels in the CoastMask-32 dataset of fictional coastal satellite tiles. Training tiles are separated from validation tiles by acquisition date. We compare the predicted cloud masks with hand-drawn reference masks using intersection over union. Thin cloud boundaries over bright sand are reviewed separately because small shifts strongly affect the overlap metric there. The model takes three visible channels and returns one cloud probability per pixel. We retain the original coastline orientation so that reviewers can locate each example on an index map.

abstracts.title: Delivery center queue under a burst
abstracts.abstract: This operations research study uses discrete-event simulation to estimate waiting times at a parcel sorting center under a bursty arrival policy. Arrivals and service durations are generated from distributions defined in the experiment. No dataset is specified. We compare two staffing schedules over identical simulated arrival sequences and repeat the comparison with several independent random seeds. The main quantity of interest is the fraction of parcels waiting longer than twenty minutes. We also track how long spare capacity sits idle and report the assumptions needed to interpret a favorable result during the first hour.

abstracts.title: Tracking a resonance from phone recordings
abstracts.abstract: In acoustics, we use the fast Fourier transform on the RoomTone-48 dataset to identify a dominant resonance in short recordings of a fictional test room. Each waveform is aligned to the same sampling rate and analyzed with overlapping windows. We compare the strongest spectral peak across microphone positions and flag clips with a weak peak relative to nearby frequencies. An annotated frequency reference allows readers to check whether the peak remains in the expected band. We retain quiet clips in the evaluation because background noise can lead to confident-looking but inconsistent resonance estimates.

abstracts.title: Ranking seasonal energy demand
abstracts.abstract: This energy systems project uses ridge regression on the CampusLoad-52 dataset to forecast peak electricity demand for a fictional campus. Input features summarize temperature, occupancy, and the previous week of power measurements. The model is trained on the earlier part of the calendar, with the most recent weeks reserved for evaluation. A persistence baseline copies the most recent observed peak. The team examines errors during holiday weeks as well as ordinary teaching weeks because occupancy can depart sharply from a typical schedule. Predictions are compared at the same forecast horizon and reported in kilowatts.

abstracts.title: Timing a tabletop orbit integrator
abstracts.abstract: In computational physics, we implemented velocity Verlet for a two-body orbit with a stated central force and initial conditions. We compare energy drift over a fixed number of revolutions as the time step decreases. No dataset is specified. The reference is the analytic orbit evaluated at matching time points. A second check repeats the integration in reverse from the computed final state to quantify accumulated roundoff and discretization effects. The small experiment is designed to separate errors from the numerical integration scheme from errors introduced when selecting or interpolating a stored reference trajectory.

abstracts.title: Clustering workshop participation patterns
abstracts.abstract: In education research, we used k-means clustering on the StudyHabits-72 dataset to group fictional weekly patterns of workshop participation. The input variables summarize completed exercises, question submissions, and time spent reviewing worked examples. We scale each variable using statistics computed from a fixed development split. To assess sensitivity, we rerun the clustering from several initial centroids and compare group assignments after matching cluster labels. The clusters describe patterns of activity in the synthetic records. We also inspect how the cluster centers move when one participation variable is omitted from the analysis.
